title: Apps to Earn Points for Rewards: 10 Options Compared
summary: Compare 10 apps to earn points for rewards, including how each earning method works, typical payout paths, and who each app suits best.
body_markdown:
Join Gerald for a new way to manage your finances.


Cash advances with no fees.


[Get Started](https://joingerald.com/#signup)


Three days before payday, the bills are already lined up, the fridge is looking thin, and your phone has a few reward apps sitting there with half-finished balances. That's the true test for **apps to earn points for rewards** . They only matter when the work is small, the payout path is clear, and the reward truly helps pay for something your household already buys.


This comparison focuses on earning methods, not popularity. Receipts, surveys, games, shopping portals, and linked accounts all move points in different ways, and each one has a different wait time, redemption minimum, and level of effort. I'll keep the trade-offs blunt, so you can tell which app fits a tight budget and which one just adds another chore to your day. For a broader loyalty context, the basic points model also shows up in[reward points setup for salons](https://bonusqr.com/loyalty-program/points-system) .

## 1. Play To Earn


Play To Earn by Gerald is the most practical option here if you need points to do more than sit in a wallet. It ties **games, surveys, and simple tasks** to store rewards, while the broader app also handles small-dollar cash advances, Buy Now Pay Later purchases, and prepaid mobile service. The useful part is the structure, because reward earning and everyday spending sit in the same place.


The trade-off is that this is not a pure points app. Gerald's setup works best when you already need essentials support, since some approved advance value has to be used first in the Cornerstore or on Cranberry Mobile before the rest becomes transferable cash. That makes the app more useful for a paycheck-to-paycheck user who wants one system for short-term spending and reward earning, and less useful for someone who only wants a simple gift-card grinder.


**Practical rule:** use Play To Earn when you want reward points to reduce future essentials, not when you want the highest possible conversion rate on a single task.


### What works and what gets in the way


- **Works well for irregular income:** the app's cash-flow tools and rewards live together, which reduces juggling.
- **Works well for essentials:** store rewards can offset future purchases instead of forcing discretionary redemptions.
- **Gets in the way for cash-only users:** the structure is built around the ecosystem, so it isn't just a straight cash-out app.
- **Gets in the way if you want instant simplicity:** you'll do better here if you can accept a guided flow rather than a bare-bones points wallet.


Website:[Gerald Play To Earn](https://joingerald.com/play-to-earn)


## 2. Fetch


Fetch is one of the cleanest receipt-scanning options because the routine is obvious, upload what you already bought and let the points accumulate. The app supports paper receipts, eligible eReceipts, brand offers, and shopping through Fetch Shop. That makes it a decent fit if you buy from a mix of grocery, household, and online retailers.


The practical limit is that generic receipts usually won't move the needle fast. Fetch works best as a steady background app, not as a fast-cash solution. If you already keep receipts, the effort stays low. If you hate scanning or you shop inconsistently, the balance will grow slowly and feel less useful.


A receipt app only helps if you submit receipts regularly. If you're the type who loses paper slips before you leave the parking lot, a portal or linked-account app will feel easier.


## 3. Swagbucks


Swagbucks has the broadest task mix on this list, which is why it's still relevant for people who want one app for several earning habits. It covers surveys, shopping, games, and other online activities, and SB points can go to gift cards or PayPal cash. That flexibility matters if your budget changes week to week and you can't count on the same routine every day.


The downside is tracking friction. Some earning paths need merchant confirmation, so points don't always post right away. That can be annoying if you're watching a small balance and expecting it to turn into something usable quickly. In these cases, people often get impatient and overestimate the speed of a diversified rewards platform.


For users who want a more structured income-style overview alongside a rewards app,[this work and income guide](https://joingerald.com/learn/work--income) is useful background. Swagbucks still makes sense when you want variety, but it works best if you're comfortable waiting on tracked purchases and offer approvals.


### Best fit and weak fit


- **Best fit:** users who rotate between surveys, shopping, and small digital tasks.
- **Best fit:** people who want PayPal alongside gift cards.
- **Weak fit:** anyone who expects instant posting on every action.
- **Weak fit:** users who don't want to follow offer rules carefully.


Website:[Swagbucks](https://www.swagbucks.com/)


## 4. MyPoints


MyPoints looks similar to Swagbucks on the surface, but the portal-style flow is the key difference. You earn by shopping through the site, taking surveys, watching content, and completing offers. It's a good match if you like seeing a merchant list first and deciding whether the purchase or task is worth it.


The biggest mistake is skipping the clickthrough step. If you don't start at MyPoints before buying, the reward often won't track. That makes it a better fit for disciplined shoppers than for casual browsers. When the portal flow is followed correctly, the earning path is easy to understand.


For budgeting, that clarity matters. People with tight cash flow don't need more “maybe later” points. They need an app with a visible trail from merchant offer to reward, and MyPoints usually feels more structured than a grab-bag task app. If you want to keep your long-term money habits organized, the[saving and investing guide](https://joingerald.com/learn/saving--investing) gives a useful parallel mindset.


## 5. Microsoft Rewards


Microsoft Rewards is the most predictable daily habit app on this list. Bing searches, quizzes, daily sets, and small Microsoft Store or Xbox-related actions create a routine that's easy to repeat without much thought. That consistency is the point. It suits people who prefer a few minutes a day instead of longer sessions.


The limitation is that available activities can change, and some rewards have caps or limited-time availability. So the app works best as a low-effort habit builder, not as a guaranteed source of the same redemption every week. If you're the kind of user who checks in during a commute or lunch break, the structure fits.


### Why it works for budget users


- **Low mental load:** the tasks are short and repetitive.
- **Good habit fit:** daily check-ins are easier than chasing larger offers.
- **Mainstream redemption:** gift-card-style rewards are familiar.
- **Not ideal for urgency:** it's a slow drip, not a fast payout.


Website:[Microsoft Rewards](https://www.microsoft.com/rewards)


## 6. Google Opinion Rewards


Google Opinion Rewards is the easiest survey app to live with because the surveys are short and the interface is stripped down. You answer a few questions, the credit lands, and you move on. For people who only have spare minutes here and there, that's the whole appeal.


The catch is variability. Survey frequency changes from user to user, so the app can feel busy one week and quiet the next. That means it's useful as a bonus-credit tool, not as the only app you rely on. It works best when you treat it like pocket change from idle time.


If you want a survey app that doesn't demand a long session, this is usually the one to keep. If you want predictable volume, it can disappoint.


Website:[Google Opinion Rewards](https://surveys.google.com/google-opinion-rewards/)


## 7. PayPal Rewards


PayPal Rewards is strongest when you already shop through PayPal and want the points flow to stay inside an ecosystem you know. Eligible offers earn PayPal Rewards points, and redemption can happen at checkout, for gift cards, or for donations. The math is also easy to follow, since the program uses a consistent points-to-dollar valuation.


The main advantage is convenience. If you're already checking out through PayPal, it's simpler than copying codes or moving rewards across different wallets. The downside is that not every purchase qualifies, and activation rules vary by channel. That makes it a solid choice for routine online shopping, but not for someone trying to force every transaction into a rewards path.


For a sharper comparison of how this stack differs from Gerald's approach, see[Gerald vs PayPal](https://joingerald.com/gerald-vs-paypal) . PayPal Rewards is better when you want checkout simplicity. Gerald is better when you want rewards tied to broader essentials support.


## 8. Mistplay


Mistplay is the most straightforward game-first app in this group. You install featured games, play them, earn Units, and redeem those Units for e-gift cards. If you already spend time on mobile games, that setup is easier to accept than surveys or receipt scanning.


The limitation is obvious. It runs on Android only, and the earnings depend on how much time you spend playing and which games are available. That makes it a decent fit for a user who already reaches for their phone to unwind, but not for someone looking for the highest-value point system. The app rewards time, not urgency.


One useful way to think about Mistplay is that it turns existing screen time into something slightly better than dead time. It won't fix a budget gap on its own, but it can convert a habit you already have into a small redemption path.


## 9. ReceiptPal


ReceiptPal is one of the simplest receipt apps to understand because the “Point Card” format gives the workflow a clear finish line. You upload paper receipts or connect eligible email and Amazon accounts, complete the card, and earn points. That structure helps people who want a visible target instead of a loose pile of scans.


The weakness is delay. You have to complete the full card, and rewards can take time to process. That's fine if you're patient and already save receipts, but it's frustrating if you want a quick balance bump after a grocery run. The app is easy to use, just not fast.


### Best use case


ReceiptPal is better than many receipt apps for people who want a light, repeatable routine. It's less useful if you want instant gratification or if your shopping receipts are irregular.


Website:[ReceiptPal](https://www.receiptpalapp.com/)


## 10. Pogo


Pogo is the most passive of the group because it can pick up earnings from linked accounts and surface opportunities automatically. It also adds surveys, screentime earnings, and location-based rewards, so the app gives you multiple ways to build balance without starting from scratch every time. For a low-friction user, that's a real advantage.


The cost is permissions. You have to connect accounts, and some rewards are time-limited claims. That trade-off is acceptable if you want automatic detection of eligible activity, but it's not for someone who's cautious about data sharing or hates app permissions. The payouts are easier to earn than with a manual receipt workflow, but they also depend on what the app can detect.


Pogo works best for people who want small, incremental rewards in the background while they do their normal shopping and phone use.
